questions.question: A fire alarm sounds while a technician at a printing plant swaps backup drives, and the drives due offsite, which hold the only current copy, sit across the room. What should the technician do FIRST?

options.A: Finish the swap, then leave by the nearest exit
options.B: Leave by the nearest exit and go to the assembly point
options.C: Collect the drives from across the room, then leave
options.D: Leave by the nearest exit, then return for the drives

questions.key_concept: In any emergency, human safety comes first: evacuate and be accounted for before thinking about equipment or data.
questions.pre_read: Notice what is at risk in the room: people, equipment and data. Rank them before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: Human safety comes before data and equipment in every continuity plan. When the alarm sounds, the first response is to leave by the nearest safe exit and report to the assembly point so everyone can be accounted for. Collecting the drives is the runner-up: losing the offsite copy would hurt recovery, but recovery plans can cope with lost data, and nothing replaces a person.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the task is nearly done. But every minute spent finishing work during a fire alarm is a minute of avoidable danger.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the copy matters to recovery. But crossing the room to fetch equipment delays evacuation; no backup is worth a person's safety.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it puts leaving first. But going back into a building during a fire alarm puts a life at risk again; emergency services decide when it is safe.

tips: Eliminate: A delays leaving to finish the task, and D sends the technician back inside, though a fire alarm means getting out and staying out.
Final two: B beats C because people come before data; fetching the drives delays evacuation, and recovery plans exist for lost data.
Exam cue: when life safety is at stake, pick the answer that protects people first. Equipment and data can be replaced or recovered.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 2.2.8 (Occupant Emergency Plan (OEP))
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'human safety comes first: account for people before saving equipment or data' (notes 2.2.2 Business Continuity vs Disaster Recovery). Calibration: people-safety-first item; the pilot item tests what makes a plan DR rather than BC. Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. questions.question: A ticket seller's maximum tolerable downtime (MTD) is 12 hours; after an outage, restoring systems takes 6 hours and checking orders before selling takes 4 more. What is the continuity coordinator's MOST accurate conclusion?

options.A: The plan meets the MTD, with 2 hours to spare
options.B: The plan meets the MTD, with 6 hours to spare
options.C: The plan misses the MTD, as the RTO must equal it
options.D: The plan misses the MTD, as checks count toward the RPO

questions.key_concept: The full time until a function resumes, restoring systems plus checking work, must fit within the maximum tolerable downtime.
questions.pre_read: Notice each time figure in the stem and what each recovery term measures.
questions.correct_explanation: Selling resumes only after the systems are restored and the orders checked: 6 + 4 = 10 hours, inside the 12-hour MTD with 2 hours to spare. The 6-hour figure is the runner-up: it counts only the system restore, but customers cannot buy until the orders are checked, and that work time must also fit inside the MTD.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the systems are back in 6 hours. But selling waits for the 4 hours of checks too, so the function returns at 10 hours.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because both are time limits. But the RTO must fit inside the MTD, normally shorter, leaving room for work such as these checks.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because order checks involve data. But the RPO measures how much recent data can be lost; it says nothing about time to resume.

tips: Eliminate: C treats the RTO as equal to the MTD, though it must fit inside it, and D puts a time-to-resume task into the RPO.
Final two: A beats B because the function is down until the checks finish; restore time plus work time must fit inside the MTD.
Exam cue: add every step until the business function works again, then compare the total with the MTD. The RPO is about data lost, not time.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 3.2.1 (Determine Business Processes and Recovery Criticality: MTD, RTO and RPO)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'RTO plus work recovery time must fit inside the MTD' (notes 2.2.4 Recovery Objectives: MTD, RTO and RPO). questions.question: A studio takes a full backup every Sunday night and a differential on all other nights. Its server fails Thursday morning; which restore is MOST efficient for the IT technician to recover Wednesday night's data?

options.A: Sunday's full backup
options.B: Sunday's full and the Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday differentials
options.C: Wednesday's differential backup
options.D: Sunday's full and Wednesday's differential

questions.key_concept: A differential backup holds all changes since the last full, so a restore needs the full plus only the latest differential.
questions.pre_read: Recall what each differential backup contains, counted from which earlier backup.
questions.correct_explanation: A differential backup holds every change since the last full backup, so Wednesday's differential already includes Monday's and Tuesday's changes. Restoring Sunday's full and then Wednesday's differential brings the server back to Wednesday night. Restoring all three differentials is the runner-up: it reaches the same state, but that is the incremental rule, and here it repeats work the last differential already covers, which only lengthens the restore.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a full backup holds everything. But it holds everything as of Sunday; changes from Monday to Wednesday would be lost.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it reaches the same Wednesday state. But each differential already holds every change since Sunday, so the two earlier ones only add restore time.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it is the newest copy. But a differential holds only changes since the full backup; without Sunday's full, most files are missing.

tips: Eliminate: A stops at Sunday and loses three days of changes, and C has the changes but not the full backup they build on.
Final two: D beats B because each differential holds all changes since the full; restoring every night's set is the incremental rule.
Exam cue: a differential restore is the full plus the latest differential; an incremental restore is the full plus every incremental since, in order.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 5.1.2 (Maintenance of Data Security, Integrity, and Backup: full, incremental and differential backups); NIST CSF 2.0 PR.DS-11 (backups of data are created, protected, maintained and tested)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'an incremental restore needs the full plus every incremental; a differential restore needs the full plus the latest differential' (notes 2.2.5 Backups: Types, the 3-2-1 Rule and Restore Testing). questions.question: Leaders ask an IT manager at a parts distributor, which runs orders at head office, to propose the cheapest site meeting its two-day recovery time objective (RTO). Which site is BEST?

options.A: A hot site with live copies of current data
options.B: A cold site that has space, power and cooling in place
options.C: A warm site with equipment ready and data to restore
options.D: A spare room in the head office with spare servers

questions.key_concept: Choose the least costly recovery site whose readiness still meets the RTO; readier sites cost more to keep.
questions.pre_read: Note the target recovery time and what the leaders asked for, then check each site against both.
questions.correct_explanation: Recovery sites trade readiness for cost. A warm site has equipment and connections in place, so restoring data can bring orders back within a day or two, at medium cost. A hot site is the runner-up: it would meet the target easily, but it costs the most to keep running, and leaders asked for the cheapest site that meets a two-day RTO.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a hot site meets a two-day target with room to spare. But it costs the most to keep ready, and leaders asked for the cheapest fit.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it is the cheapest site. But it must be equipped from scratch, which usually takes a week or more, too slow for a two-day target.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it costs little and is close by. But a fire or flood at head office would take out the spare room too.

tips: Eliminate: B must be equipped from scratch, usually a week or more, missing the target, and D shares the main site, so one disaster hits both.
Final two: C beats A because both meet two days, but the warm site does it at lower cost; match the site to the RTO.
Exam cue: hot sites recover in hours or less, warm in about a day to a few days, cold in weeks. Pick the cheapest that still meets the RTO.

questions.question: At a marketing agency, senior managers skip the security awareness sessions every employee must attend, and staff attendance has fallen since. What should the awareness lead propose FIRST?

options.A: Ask senior managers to attend and speak at the sessions
options.B: Send staff firmer reminders that attendance is required
options.C: Tie each employee's yearly bonus to their attendance
options.D: Cancel the sessions, as falling attendance shows little interest

questions.key_concept: Leaders set security culture by example; when they skip required activities staff follow, so leadership participation comes first.
questions.pre_read: Notice who stopped attending first and what happened to everyone else afterward.
questions.correct_explanation: Staff copy what leaders do: when senior managers skip required sessions, everyone learns the rule is optional. The cause is the example at the top, so the first fix is leaders taking part visibly, attending and speaking. Firmer reminders to staff are the runner-up: they press on the symptom, while the managers' absence keeps teaching the opposite lesson.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: reminders do reinforce the rule. But they target staff while leaders keep skipping, so the message that sessions are optional continues.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because money motivates. But penalties build resentment, not culture, and they leave leaders still setting the opposite example.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because low attendance looks like low interest. But attendance fell after managers stopped going; the cause is their example, not the sessions.

tips: Eliminate: C leans on penalties, which build fear rather than security culture, and D drops required training because of a symptom.
Final two: A beats B because the cause is the leaders' example; reminders to staff treat the symptom while managers keep skipping.
Exam cue: security culture starts at the top. When leaders exempt themselves, fix their visible example before pressing everyone else.

questions.question: A city parking officer finds new quick response (QR) code stickers on pay machines that send drivers to a look-alike payment site. Which type of attack is this MOST accurately?

options.A: A smishing attack
options.B: A quishing attack
options.C: A vishing attack
options.D: A whaling attack

questions.key_concept: Phishing variants are named by channel or by target; a QR code that leads to a fake site is quishing.
questions.pre_read: Ask how the lure reaches its victims: by text, by call, by a scanned code or by targeting someone senior.
questions.correct_explanation: Quishing is phishing through a QR code: scanning it opens a fake site that collects payment or login details, and stickers placed over genuine codes are a common method. Smishing is the runner-up: victims also land on a fake site on their phone, but smishing arrives by text message, and here the lure is a printed code on the machine.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the fake site opens on a phone. But smishing arrives as a text message; this lure is a printed code that drivers scan.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it is another phone-based scam. But vishing uses voice calls, and no one here is called.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it is a named variant. But whaling targets senior executives; these stickers target any driver who parks.

tips: Eliminate: C needs a voice call, and D targets executives; neither fits a printed code aimed at any driver.
Final two: B beats A because the lure arrives through a scanned code, not a text message; smishing is named for SMS.
Exam cue: most phishing variants are named by channel: smishing by text, vishing by voice, quishing by QR code. Whaling and spear phishing are named by target.

questions.question: At a design agency's badge-controlled door, someone in a contractor's high-visibility vest carrying a ladder asks an employee to hold it open. What is the employee's BEST response?

options.A: Hold the door and help carry the ladder inside
options.B: Check the contractor's ID card, then hold the door
options.C: Let them in, then report it if they act oddly
options.D: Direct them to reception to sign in and be collected

questions.key_concept: Never let unbadged people through a controlled door; send them to reception, because uniforms and ID cards are easy to fake.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the person is asking for, and what the badge reader on the door is meant to check.
questions.correct_explanation: Holding a controlled door for someone without a badge is piggybacking, and a work vest and a ladder are a classic way to get it. The safe, polite answer is to send them to reception, where visits are checked and staff come to collect them. Checking their ID card is the runner-up: it feels like verification, but the card comes from the visitor and is easy to fake.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because helping is polite. But holding a controlled door lets an unverified person past the badge reader, which is exactly what the disguise is for.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: checking ID feels careful. But the visitor supplies the card and it is easy to fake; verification needs a channel the organization controls.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because reporting is good practice. But once inside, an intruder can act at once; the badge reader exists to stop entry, not record it.

tips: Eliminate: A lets an unverified person past the badge reader, and C reports only after access is already given.
Final two: D beats B because verification must come through a channel you trust; an ID card the visitor carries proves little.
Exam cue: uniforms, ladders and urgency are props. Send anyone without a badge to the proper check-in point instead of judging them yourself.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AT-2(3) (Literacy Training and Awareness | Social Engineering and Mining); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PE-3 (Physical Access Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'verify through a separate known channel and follow procedure' (notes 2.3.3 Social Engineering Tactics). Angle: in-person piggybacking; the pilot items test quid pro quo and phone requests. Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Standards audit fix (30 Oct 2026): re-set away from cc_d5_043's courier prop.

questions.subtopic: 2.3 Security awareness. AI-boosted phishing and deepfakes
questions.question: A regional broadcaster's awareness course still teaches staff to spot phishing by spelling mistakes, though attackers now use AI to write fluent lures. Which change should the awareness lead make FIRST?

options.A: Add AI-written examples so staff learn to spot their style
options.B: Install an AI-text detector on email and retire the old course
options.C: Teach staff to verify unusual requests through known channels
options.D: Run the existing course twice a year instead of once

questions.key_concept: AI makes phishing fluent, so awareness training should teach verifying requests through known channels, not judging spelling or style.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the course teaches staff to look for, and what attackers can now do about it.
questions.correct_explanation: AI tools now write fluent, personal messages, so polish no longer separates real from fake. Training should shift from how a message looks to what it asks: an unusual payment, password or urgent request gets checked through a channel the staff member already trusts. Teaching AI writing style is the runner-up: it still judges polish, and AI text is too varied to spot reliably.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: real AI examples belong in training. But spotting AI style is unreliable; staff need a habit that works however polished the message is.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a tool scales. But AI-text detectors miss much and flag genuine mail; no filter replaces people who verify odd requests.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because repetition builds habits. But repeating outdated advice twice as often teaches the wrong habit twice as well.

tips: Eliminate: B hands judgment to an unreliable detector and drops training, and D repeats outdated content more often.
Final two: C beats A because verification works on any lure; judging writing style fails once AI makes lures fluent.
Exam cue: against AI-written lures and deepfakes, teach process, not polish. Check the request through a known channel before acting.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 600-1 (Generative AI Profile) Section 2.9 (Information Security: generative AI may augment attacks such as hacking, malware and phishing); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AT-2(6) (Literacy Training and Awareness | Cyber Threat Environment)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'awareness content shows real AI examples to prove polish is no longer a clue, and teaches verifying requests through known channels' (notes 2.3.5 AI-Boosted Phishing and Deepfakes). Angle: updating training content; the pilot item and the notes example test a deepfake video call. Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Provenance fix (31 Oct 2026): quote matches the revised notes 2.3.5 bullet.

questions.question: A shop assistant must set a new password for the store's ordering system, which accepts up to 64 characters. Which choice BEST follows current password advice?

options.A: A 24-character phrase of four randomly chosen words
options.B: Eight characters mixing symbols, numbers and capital letters
options.C: The old password with its final number raised by one
options.D: A favorite team's name with the current year added

questions.key_concept: Length beats complexity: a long passphrase of random words is stronger and easier to remember than a short complex password.
questions.pre_read: Notice the length the system allows, and compare how hard each choice would be to guess.
questions.correct_explanation: Length does most of the work: four random words make a long passphrase that is hard to guess and easy to remember, and current guidance favors length over forced complexity. The eight-character mixed password is the runner-up: symbols look strong, but short passwords fall quickly to guessing tools, and people tend to use predictable patterns, such as a capital first and a number last.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: mixed characters feel strong. But eight characters is short, people follow predictable patterns, and length adds far more strength.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it is easy to remember. But attackers who know an old password try small changes like this first.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it is personal. But team names and years are common, and easy to find on social media.

tips: Eliminate: C changes one predictable character of a known password, and D uses public, common details attackers try early.
Final two: A beats B because length beats complexity; a long passphrase resists guessing far better than eight mixed characters.
Exam cue: when a system allows long passwords, choose length, such as several random words. Keep each one unique, in a password manager.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-63B-4 (Authentication and Authenticator Management: password requirements)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'length beats complexity' (notes 2.3.6 Password and Passphrase Habits). Angle: choosing a password; the pilot item tests sharing a password with a caller and the notes example tests reuse. Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.question: During a restructuring at a car manufacturer, the awareness lead drafts a phishing simulation announcing surprise job cuts, expecting high engagement. Which step for the plan is BEST?

options.A: Send the job-cut lure only to staff who clicked before
options.B: Announce the test date so staff know to watch for it
options.C: Keep the job-cut lure, since realistic tests teach the most
options.D: Replace it with a realistic lure, such as a parcel notice

questions.key_concept: Phishing simulations should be realistic but must avoid lures that cause real distress, since trust drives reporting.
questions.pre_read: Notice what is happening to staff right now, and how this lure would land on them.
questions.correct_explanation: Simulations exist to build skills and trust. A lure about job cuts during a real restructuring causes genuine fear and anger that outlast the test and damage reporting, while a realistic lure without that harm still teaches staff to spot phishing. Keeping the job-cut lure is the runner-up: realism matters, but realism bought with real distress costs more trust than it teaches.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because past clickers need practice. But aiming a distressing lure at them feels punitive and makes them less likely to report.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because warning staff seems fair. But staff then watch only on that day; saying that tests happen at random is enough.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: realistic lures do teach well. But this one exploits a real fear during real job changes, damaging trust in the security team.

tips: Eliminate: A singles out past clickers, which reads as punishment, and B announces the date, which turns the test into a memory exercise.
Final two: D beats C because simulations must teach without real harm; a job-cut lure during restructuring costs the trust reporting depends on.
Exam cue: good simulations are realistic, approved in advance, no-blame and never cruel. Trust is what makes people report real attacks.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AT-2(1) (Literacy Training and Awareness | Practical Exercises); NIST SP 800-50 Rev. 1 Section 2.7.2 (Experiential Learning: phishing exercises reviewed in advance, run at random and never punitive)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'simulations avoid lures that cause real distress and treat a click as a teaching moment' (notes 2.3.7 Reporting Culture and Phishing Simulations). Angle: lure design; the pilot item tests naming clickers. Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Standards audit fix (30 Oct 2026): key no longer the only negated option; citation paraphrase matches what the section says.

questions.question: A software reseller's phishing report rate jumped from 20% to 55% once reports from a new email button were counted with help desk calls. What should the reporting analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Present the rise as proof that awareness training is working
options.B: Note the counting change and mark where the trend restarts
options.C: Report the new count as usual, as the data is more complete
options.D: Drop the metric, since its figures can no longer be trusted

questions.key_concept: Metrics must be collected the same way each period; when the method changes, record it and restart the baseline.
questions.pre_read: Notice what changed at the same moment the number jumped.
questions.correct_explanation: A metric is comparable over time only if it is measured the same way. Counting button reports as well as calls changed the method, so much of the jump may reflect the new count, not new behavior. The analyst notes the change and marks the break. Reporting the new figure as usual is the runner-up: the data is better, but a silent method change makes the jump look like progress.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the number moved the right way. But the counting changed at the same time, so the rise cannot be credited to training.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the new data is more complete. But changing the method without a note makes old and new figures look comparable when they are not.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the trend broke. But the metric is still useful; noting the change and building a new baseline keeps it meaningful.

tips: Eliminate: A credits training with a rise the new counting may explain, and D drops a useful metric instead of noting the method change.
Final two: B beats C because a quiet method change breaks the trend; better data still needs a note so readers compare like with like.
Exam cue: when the way a number is counted changes, record the change and restart the baseline. Comparable beats impressive.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 3.2 (Characteristics of Measures: consistency, time-based reference and replicability); NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 2.4 (Metrics: key risk indicators and key performance indicators)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'collect data the same way every period, so trends mean something' (notes 2.4.1 Measures and Metrics: The Basics). Angle: a method change breaking a trend, not the notes example of replacing a vanity count. Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2.4 Measuring effectiveness. Using measurement to improve
questions.question: A cruise line's server team took 40 days on average to apply critical patches, against a 14-day target, so the IT manager added a weekly patch window. What is the metrics analyst's BEST next step?

options.A: Mark the patching gap closed now the window is in place
options.B: Raise the target to 40 days to match current results
options.C: Track patch times over the coming months against the target
options.D: Add three new patch metrics to the server team's monthly dashboard

questions.key_concept: After a fix, measure again against the target before closing the issue; a process change is not proof of a better outcome.
questions.pre_read: Notice what has changed so far: the process, or the result.
questions.correct_explanation: A fix is an expectation until the numbers confirm it. The analyst keeps measuring patch times against the 14-day target over the next few months to see whether the weekly window closes the gap, and reports the result to the IT manager. Marking the gap closed is the runner-up: the fix is in place, but a change in process is not yet a change in outcome.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a fix has been made. But nobody yet knows whether patches now land within 14 days; closing the gap before measuring assumes success.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the metric would turn green. But moving the target to match poor results hides the risk instead of reducing it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because more data seems helpful. But the existing metric already answers the question; more charts do not show whether the fix worked.

tips: Eliminate: B moves the target to fit the problem, and D adds metrics when the existing one already answers the question.
Final two: C beats A because only a new measurement shows whether the fix worked; a process change is not yet a better outcome.
Exam cue: improvement is a loop. Find the cause, fix it with an owner, then measure again before calling it done.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.OV-03 (organizational cybersecurity risk management performance is evaluated and reviewed for adjustments needed); NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 4.4 (Evaluating Methods for Supporting Continuous Improvement: leading and lagging indicators)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'give each fix an owner and a due date, then measure again to confirm it worked' (notes 2.4.6 Using Measurement to Improve). Angle: confirming a fix by measuring again, not the notes example of metric gaming. Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Cross-review fix (31 Oct 2026): option D names the server team's dashboard so the key is not the longest option (CD-14).

questions.question: A rail operator's IT team tracks the share of new starters with working accounts on day one, against a 95% service target. What is this metric MOST accurately?

options.A: A key risk indicator warning of rising exposure
options.B: A risk appetite statement set by the board
options.C: A risk tolerance limit for a single named risk
options.D: A key performance indicator tracking a goal

questions.key_concept: A KPI measures a process against its goal; a KRI warns that a named risk is growing toward its tolerance.
questions.pre_read: Ask what this figure is compared with, and what anyone would do if it dropped.
questions.correct_explanation: A key performance indicator shows how well a process meets its goal, and this one compares day-one accounts with a 95% service target. If it falls, the fix is to improve onboarding. The key risk indicator is the runner-up: the same kind of number can be a KRI, but only when it warns that a named risk is growing toward its limit, and this one judges service delivery.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: KPIs and KRIs can look alike. But this figure is judged against a service target, which makes it a measure of performance, not an early warning.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it involves a target. But an appetite statement is the board's broad view of how much risk to take, not a measured result.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because 95% sounds like a limit. But a tolerance bounds a risk; this number measures how well a service is delivered.

tips: Eliminate: B and C are risk limits that leaders set, not measured results, so neither describes a figure tracked against a target.
Final two: D beats A because the figure judges a process against its goal; a KRI warns that a named risk is getting worse.
Exam cue: ask what the number is judged against. A goal or service target makes it a KPI; a risk and its tolerance make it a KRI.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 4.4 (Evaluating Methods for Supporting Continuous Improvement: leading and lagging indicators); NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 2.4 (Metrics: key risk indicators and key performance indicators)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'the same number can be either; what matters is whether it judges performance or warns of risk' (notes 2.4.3 Key Performance and Key Risk Indicators). Angle: recognizing a KPI; the pilot item asks for the best KRI. Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.question: After a competitor's breach, a retailer's leaders lower the tolerance for unpatched payment systems, and only the risk owner may approve key risk indicator (KRI) thresholds. What should the dashboard analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Ask the risk owner to sign off thresholds matching the new tolerance
options.B: Tell the risk owner the current thresholds still fit the new tolerance
options.C: Tighten the dashboard's thresholds to match the leaders' new tolerance
options.D: Add a KRI that tracks news coverage of the competitor's payment breach

questions.key_concept: KRI thresholds are set from risk tolerance; when tolerance changes, the thresholds are revised and approved by whoever owns them.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the leaders changed and who approves the numbers on the dashboard.
questions.correct_explanation: Thresholds are where a tolerance meets the dashboard: when leaders change the tolerance, the thresholds must change with it, or the colors keep judging the old limit. Here only the risk owner may approve thresholds, so the analyst proposes new ones for approval. Tightening them directly is the runner-up: the numbers may be right, but changing approved limits alone bypasses the owner's decision.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because nothing has turned red. But the colors are judged against the old tolerance; under the new one, today's green may already be too much risk.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the thresholds do need tightening. But here only the risk owner may approve them; an analyst changing limits alone bypasses that decision.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the breach prompted the change. But news about another firm is not a measure of this retailer's own unpatched systems.

tips: Eliminate: B judges risk against a tolerance leaders have replaced, and D tracks news about another firm instead of the retailer's own exposure.
Final two: A beats C because only the risk owner may approve thresholds here; the analyst proposes the change rather than making it alone.
Exam cue: thresholds come from tolerance. When the tolerance, the business or the threats change, revisit the thresholds with whoever owns them.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RM-02 (risk appetite and risk tolerance statements are established, communicated and maintained); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PM-6 (Measures of Performance)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'thresholds come from the risk appetite and tolerance leaders agreed, and are reviewed when they change' (notes 2.4.4 Thresholds, Targets and Escalation). Angle: a tolerance change; the pilot item tests escalating a red KRI. Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Standards audit fix (30 Oct 2026): stem no longer reads as if the owner already approved new thresholds; leaders, not the board, set tolerance. Cross-review fix (31 Oct 2026): pre_read says leaders, as the stem does (CD-19); the explanation and tip rest on the stem's own approval rule, matching notes 2.4.4 (named threshold owner).

questions.question: A patent firm's AI policy allows two approved assistants, and its security team wants a key risk indicator (KRI) for client data leaking through other AI tools. Which measure BEST fits?

options.A: Staff completion rate for the AI policy course
options.B: Weekly visits from firm devices to unapproved AI services
options.C: Number of licenses bought for the approved assistants
options.D: Number of help desk tickets about approved assistants

questions.key_concept: An AI risk indicator should track the risky behavior itself, such as use of unapproved AI tools, not training completion.
questions.pre_read: Name the risk in the stem, then ask which number would rise before that risk turns into harm.
questions.correct_explanation: A KRI should warn early that a named risk is growing. Visits to unapproved AI services measure the very behavior that leaks client data, and a rising count signals trouble before a breach. Course completion is the runner-up: training supports the policy, but completion shows who sat the course, not whether anyone is pasting client files into other tools.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: training supports the AI policy. But completion is an implementation measure; it shows who finished a course, not whether staff use unapproved tools.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because licenses show adoption. But buying licenses for approved tools says nothing about use of the unapproved ones that leak data.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because tickets show how staff use AI. But support requests about approved tools measure their usability, not leakage elsewhere.

tips: Eliminate: C and D measure the approved assistants, while the risk sits in tools outside the approved list.
Final two: B beats A because a KRI tracks the risky behavior itself; course completion shows training happened, not that behavior changed.
Exam cue: a good AI KRI measures the behavior or condition that creates the risk, such as unapproved tool use, drift or rising overrides.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 4.4 (Evaluating Methods for Supporting Continuous Improvement: leading and lagging indicators); NIST CSF 2.0 DE.CM-03 (personnel activity and technology usage are monitored to find potentially adverse events)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'use of unapproved AI tools shows policy risk' (notes 2.4.7 AI Risk Indicators). Angle: unapproved AI tool use as a KRI; the pilot item tests a rising override rate. Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A museum passed its yearly card-payment compliance assessment, and its director tells the security analyst that the museum's security risks are now handled. Which reply is MOST accurate?

options.A: Only the systems outside card payments still need a risk review
options.B: Card rules were met at that point, but risks still need managing
options.C: Passing shows the museum's risks are within appetite for the year
options.D: The risks are handled, as long as a compliance tool tracks results

questions.key_concept: Compliance shows set obligations were met at a point in time; it does not prove an organization, or even one system, is secure.
questions.pre_read: Think about what a passed compliance assessment checks, and what it leaves out.
questions.correct_explanation: Compliance shows that set obligations, here the card rules, were met when the assessment ran. It does not mean the museum's risks are handled: risks outside those rules, new threats and changes since the test all remain, so risk management carries on. The runner-up still treats the card systems as finished, but even inside its scope a pass reflects one point in time.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: other systems do need review. But a pass shows card rules were met at one point in time; card systems still need their risks managed too.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a pass feels like a clean bill of health. But compliance checks set rules at one point in time; it says nothing about whether risk sits within appetite.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because tools make tracking easier. But a tool records results; risks are handled by owners making decisions, not by tracking.

tips: Eliminate: C reads a pass as proof that risk sits within appetite all year, and D credits a tool with handling risk, which takes owners and decisions.
Final two: B beats A because a pass proves obligations were met at a point in time, not that even the card systems are done with risk review.
Exam cue: compliant is not the same as secure. Compliance proves set duties were met; risk management keeps going after any pass.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.OC-03 (legal, regulatory and contractual requirements, including privacy obligations, are understood and managed); NIST SP 800-39 Section 3.4 (Monitoring Risk)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Compliance confirms obligations are met and keeps the evidence to prove it', with the trap 'being compliant means the organization is secure' (notes 2.1.1 GRC Purpose and Importance). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A theater company's program owner sets its governance, risk and compliance (GRC) scope, and a junior analyst finds donor card details in a fundraising tool left out of it. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Add the tool to the scope, then inform the program owner
options.B: Leave the tool out, since the approved scope does not cover it
options.C: Delete the card details from the tool to end the exposure
options.D: Report the card data found outside the scope to the program owner

questions.key_concept: A GRC program's scope is set by its owner; practitioners report sensitive data found outside it instead of changing the scope themselves.
questions.pre_read: Notice who sets the program's scope and what the analyst found outside it.
questions.correct_explanation: Scope decides which systems and data the program protects and measures, and here the program owner sets it. Card data in an unlisted tool is a real gap, so the analyst reports it with the details and lets the owner decide whether to widen the scope or move the data. Adding the tool themselves is the runner-up: the gap is real, but changing scope is the owner's call, not the analyst's.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the tool probably does belong in scope. But the program owner sets the scope here; the analyst reports the gap rather than widening it alone.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the scope was approved. But sensitive data outside it is exactly the gap a scope check should catch, not a reason to look away.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it ends the exposure fast. But deleting business records is not the analyst's decision, and the data may be needed or need secure handling.

tips: Eliminate: B treats the approved scope as the limit of what to report, though sensitive data outside it is a gap, and C destroys records the analyst has no authority to delete.
Final two: D beats A because the program owner sets the scope; the analyst brings the gap to them instead of changing the scope alone.
Exam cue: when sensitive data turns up outside a program's scope, report it to whoever sets the scope. Scope is a governance decision, not a technical one.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 ID.AM-07 (inventories of data and corresponding metadata for designated data types are maintained); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-02 (roles, responsibilities and authorities related to cybersecurity risk management are established, communicated, understood and enforced)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Set the scope, meaning which units, systems and data are covered' (notes 2.1.2 Planning a GRC Program). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.question: Mapping a payroll software firm's controls to the NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0, the compliance analyst finds four outcomes that apply but lack a control. What should the analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Plan new or extended controls for those four outcomes only
options.B: Build a separate CSF control set beside the existing controls
options.C: Mark the four outcomes not applicable to complete the mapping
options.D: Buy a compliance tool that maps the CSF outcomes automatically

questions.key_concept: Mapping existing controls to a new framework reuses them; relevant items with no control are gaps to close, not items to exclude.
questions.pre_read: Notice which outcomes are relevant and which already have a control.
questions.correct_explanation: A crosswalk lets one control set show progress against several frameworks, so the existing controls carry over and only the real gaps need work. Four relevant outcomes with no control are gaps, so the analyst proposes new or extended controls for them. Marking them not applicable is the runner-up: tailoring is allowed, but only with a true reason, and these outcomes do apply.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the CSF is new to the firm. But a crosswalk reuses one control set; a second set doubles the work and the evidence.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: frameworks do allow tailoring. But not applicable needs a true reason, and these outcomes are relevant; marking them hides real gaps.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a tool speeds up mapping. But it only records which controls meet which outcomes; it cannot supply the four missing controls.

tips: Eliminate: B builds a duplicate control set where one mapped set serves both, and D buys a tool that can map controls but cannot create missing ones.
Final two: A beats C because not applicable is for outcomes that truly do not apply; relevant outcomes without a control are gaps to close.
Exam cue: map once, reuse the evidence and treat only the unmet items as gaps. Every exclusion needs a real, recorded reason.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 Section 3.1 (CSF Profiles: Organizational Profiles are used to understand, tailor, assess, prioritize and communicate outcomes); NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2 Task S-2 (Control Tailoring)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'A crosswalk maps one framework to another, so one control shows progress against both' (notes 2.1.5 Choosing and Mapping Frameworks in GRC). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A governance, risk and compliance (GRC) platform shows 30% of staff have not acknowledged the security manager's new acceptable use policy; the procedure assigns follow-up to the GRC analyst. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Mark the policy acknowledged for everyone, since it was emailed to all
options.B: Ask the security manager to chase the staff who have not acknowledged
options.C: Send reminders to staff who have not acknowledged and track replies
options.D: Turn off the acknowledgment check until the policy's next version

questions.key_concept: GRC tools track policy acknowledgments; when the procedure assigns follow-up to the practitioner, they act on the gap rather than pass it up.
questions.pre_read: Notice who owns the policy and who the procedure gives the follow-up to.
questions.correct_explanation: The procedure gives follow-up to the analyst, so chasing the missing acknowledgments is in-role work: send reminders, track who replies and report what is left. The policy owner set the rule, not the follow-up task. Asking the security manager to chase staff is the runner-up: the owner should hear about stubborn gaps, but handing back a task the procedure assigns to the analyst only delays it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because everyone received the policy. But an acknowledgment records that each person read and agreed to it; a sent email is not that record.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the security manager owns the policy. But the procedure assigns follow-up to the analyst, so passing it back delays work the analyst should do.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it clears the red figure. But hiding the check hides the gap; the platform should show it until staff acknowledge.

tips: Eliminate: A counts a sent email as agreement, and D silences the check so the gap leaves the screen instead of closing.
Final two: C beats B because the procedure assigns follow-up to the analyst; owning a policy does not mean doing every task under it.
Exam cue: a named owner does not always mean escalate. When the procedure assigns the task to you, do it, and keep the owner informed of what remains.

questions.question: A key risk indicator shows a brewery's supplier-portal risk now exceeds its tolerance, and the risk owner, the purchasing manager, asks an analyst to record it as accepted. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Record the acceptance with the owner's signature and a review date
options.B: Raise the entry's tolerance so the current level falls within it
options.C: Route the acceptance decision to senior management for review
options.D: Close the register entry once the owner accepts the risk

questions.key_concept: Risk owners accept risk within tolerance; a risk beyond tolerance goes to senior management to accept or treat further.
questions.pre_read: Notice where the risk sits against its tolerance, and who is asking to accept it.
questions.correct_explanation: A risk owner may accept risk only within the tolerance leaders set. This risk is already beyond tolerance, so the decision to accept it or treat it further belongs to senior management, and the analyst routes it there with the indicator data. Recording the owner's acceptance is the runner-up: that is the right step within tolerance, but here it would let one manager accept more risk than leaders allowed.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: within tolerance, a signed acceptance with a review date is exactly right. But this risk exceeds tolerance, which puts the decision above the risk owner.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it makes the register consistent. But leaders set tolerances; moving the limit to fit the risk hides the breach instead of deciding it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because acceptance can feel final. But accepted risks stay open with a review date, and this acceptance is not the owner's to give.

tips: Eliminate: B moves a tolerance leaders set to fit the risk, and D treats acceptance as closing the risk, when accepted risks stay on the register for review.
Final two: C beats A because a risk owner accepts only within tolerance; beyond it, senior management decides whether to accept or treat.
Exam cue: within tolerance, the risk owner accepts; beyond tolerance, senior management decides. The analyst records and routes, and never accepts risk.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-39 Section 3.3 (Responding to Risk: accept, avoid, mitigate, share or transfer); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RM-02 (risk appetite and risk tolerance statements are established, communicated and maintained)

questions.question: After staff at a recruitment agency pasted candidate resumes into free AI chatbots, the chief executive wants every AI tool banned. Which approach should the security manager propose as BEST?

options.A: Approve vetted AI tools with clear data rules and usage monitoring
options.B: Block every AI service on the network and staff devices, as requested
options.C: Remind staff by email not to paste candidate data into chatbots
options.D: Let each team pick its own AI tools once names are removed

questions.key_concept: Governing AI use means approved tools, data rules and monitoring under an approved policy; blanket bans push staff toward unseen tools.
questions.pre_read: Notice what caused the leak and what the chief executive asked for.
questions.correct_explanation: Blanket bans tend to push staff toward hidden tools on personal devices, where the agency sees nothing. A governed approach gives staff vetted tools, rules on what data each may handle and monitoring, under a policy senior management approves. Banning everything is the runner-up: it answers the chief executive's request, but it treats the symptom and leaves the need, and the leak risk, unmanaged.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it stops the known leaks, as the chief executive asked. But staff who still need AI turn to unseen tools, so the risk moves out of view.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because staff need to know the rule. But a reminder alone gives no safe tool and no data rules, so the same pressure leads to the same leaks.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because removing names lowers exposure. But unvetted tools may keep or train on what staff paste, and resumes hold far more than names.

tips: Eliminate: C relies on a reminder with no approved tool or data rules, and D lets each team pick unvetted tools with only names removed.
Final two: A beats B because approved tools, data rules and monitoring manage the risk, while a blanket ban drives AI use out of sight.
Exam cue: for AI use, govern rather than ban: approved tools, clear data rules and monitoring, under a policy leaders approve.

questions.question: A cinema chain's ticketing system has a standby server, but only one network technician knows the manual steps to switch over to it. What should the IT manager propose to BEST improve availability?

options.A: Give the technician an on-call phone and a spare work laptop
options.B: Add a second standby server next to the existing one
options.C: Take ticketing database backups every hour instead of nightly
options.D: Write failover instructions and cross-train a colleague

questions.key_concept: A single point of failure can be a person; documented steps and a trained alternate keep failover working.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the switch-over depends on.
questions.correct_explanation: The standby server removes one single point of failure, but the one person who can use it is another. Written steps and a second trained technician mean the switch-over still works when that person is sick, away or unreachable. Making the technician easier to reach is the runner-up: it shortens delays, but service still depends on one person being available at the moment of failure.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: faster contact does help in an outage. But the service still depends on one person, who may be ill, on leave or unreachable.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because spares improve availability. But a second spare needs the same manual switch-over, which still only one person can do.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because backups protect data. But backup frequency limits data loss; it does not bring service back while no one can run the switch-over.

tips: Eliminate: B adds hardware that the same single person must still switch over, and C changes how much data could be lost, not how fast service returns.
Final two: D beats A because a second trained person removes the single point of failure, while a phone only makes one person easier to reach.
Exam cue: single points of failure include people. Look for the one person, link or device everything depends on, and add a second.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 3.4.6 (Roles and Responsibilities: teams stay viable when members are unavailable, or alternates are designated); NIST CSF 2.0 PR.IR-03 (mechanisms are implemented to achieve resilience requirements in normal and adverse situations)

questions.question: A theme park's continuity coordinator asks function owners to rate how harm grows during outages for a business impact analysis (BIA). Which outage should the BIA rate MOST severe?

options.A: Online ticket sales stop, so the year's busiest weekend loses its sales
options.B: Ride sensor monitoring stops, so operators cannot see ride faults
options.C: Staff payroll runs two days late, so wages reach accounts late
options.D: The park news blog goes offline, so visitors miss updates

questions.key_concept: A BIA rates how harm grows when each function stops; outages that put people at risk rank above financial loss.
questions.pre_read: Notice what each outage would stop, and what could follow from it.
questions.correct_explanation: A BIA rates the harm each outage causes over time, and harm to people is the most severe kind. Without ride sensor monitoring, faults that could injure riders go unseen, so that function ranks above any revenue loss. Lost ticket sales on the busiest weekend is the runner-up: the money is real and grows by the hour, but it can be recovered in a way an injury cannot.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: lost sales on a peak weekend are a serious impact. But money can be recovered; a ride fault no one can see can injure people.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because every employee is affected. But a two-day pay delay is limited and recoverable, far below a risk to riders' safety.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because visitors notice it. But a news blog outage causes little harm, even over days, and can wait behind critical functions.

tips: Eliminate: C is a short, recoverable delay, and D is a low-impact outage that can wait for days.
Final two: B beats A because harm to people outranks lost revenue when a BIA rates impact.
Exam cue: in any ranking of impact, people's safety comes first. Then weigh how fast harm grows for money, obligations and reputation.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Appendix B (Sample BIA Template: impact categories can include harm to individuals); NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 3.2.1 (Determine Business Processes and Recovery Criticality: MTD, RTO and RPO)

questions.question: A ferry operator copies its booking database every 6 hours, against a 30-minute recovery point objective (RPO); IT proposes a hot site loaded from those same copies. What is the continuity coordinator's MOST accurate conclusion?

options.A: The hot site cuts downtime, but the copies still miss the RPO
options.B: The hot site meets the RPO, but needs a full test first
options.C: The copies meet the RPO if a restore finishes within 30 minutes
options.D: The RPO should move to 6 hours so it matches the copies

questions.key_concept: The RPO depends on how recent the last good copy is; a faster recovery site shortens downtime but not data loss.
questions.pre_read: Work out how much booking data could be lost at worst, then ask what a hot site changes.
questions.correct_explanation: The RPO looks back: with copies every 6 hours, up to 6 hours of bookings can be lost, far beyond the 30-minute limit. A hot site speeds the return to service, which helps the RTO, but it restores the same old copy. Only more frequent copies or replication close the RPO gap. The runner-up mixes the two targets: restore speed is about time, not about how much data is lost.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a hot site is the fastest recovery option and testing matters. But it loads the same 6-hour-old copies, so no test changes how much data is lost.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: restore speed does matter. But a fast restore meets the RTO; the RPO depends on how recent the copy is, and 6 hours is far over 30 minutes.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it closes the gap. But the business sets the RPO from its needs; the coordinator reports the gap rather than bending the target to fit the copies.

tips: Eliminate: B credits a hot site with reducing data loss, and D bends the business's target to fit the current copies.
Final two: A beats C because restore speed meets the RTO; only more frequent copies or replication change how much data is lost.
Exam cue: RPO looks back to the last good copy; RTO looks forward to service returning. Sites fix time; backups and replication fix data loss.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 3.2.1 (Determine Business Processes and Recovery Criticality: MTD, RTO and RPO); NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 3.4.3 (Alternate Sites)

questions.question: A translation agency's nightly backups go to a storage server that its domain administrator accounts can delete, and ransomware groups now target backups. Which change should the system administrator propose as BEST?

options.A: Encrypt the backup files so attackers cannot read them
options.B: Run the backups every hour instead of every night
options.C: Keep one backup copy immutable for a fixed retention period
options.D: Add a nightly copy to a domain-joined server at another office

questions.key_concept: At least one backup copy should be offline or immutable, so ransomware or a stolen administrator account cannot alter or delete it.
questions.pre_read: Notice who can delete the backups today and what attackers go after.
questions.correct_explanation: Ransomware crews look for backups and use stolen administrator accounts to delete or encrypt them before striking. A copy that is immutable, or offline, cannot be changed even by an administrator account, so a clean restore stays possible. Copying to a domain-joined server at another office is the runner-up: it adds an offsite copy, as the 3-2-1 rule asks, but the same domain administrator accounts could still delete it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because encryption keeps backups from being read. But attackers who can delete or overwrite the copies do not need to read them.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because more frequent copies lose less data. But every copy sits on the same deletable server, so ransomware can still wipe them all.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: it adds an offsite copy, as 3-2-1 asks. But the same domain administrator accounts can delete a domain-joined server's copy, so one stolen account destroys every copy.

tips: Eliminate: A protects confidentiality when the threat is deletion, and B changes how much data could be lost, not whether the copies survive.
Final two: C beats D because an immutable copy survives a stolen administrator account; a domain-joined server at another office does not.
Exam cue: 3-2-1 is a start. Keep at least one copy offline or immutable, beyond the reach of any account an attacker could steal.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CP-9 (System Backup); NIST CSF 2.0 PR.DS-11 (backups of data are created, protected, maintained and tested)

questions.question: A national lottery operator's continuity coordinator wants to prove its draw system runs at the recovery site while the main site keeps working normally. Which plan test BEST fits this goal?

options.A: A tabletop exercise where the team talks through the plan
options.B: A checklist review where each team checks its plan section
options.C: A full interruption test where production at the main site stops
options.D: A parallel test where the standby site runs beside production

questions.key_concept: A parallel test runs systems at the recovery site while production continues; a full interruption test shuts production down.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the coordinator must prove and what must keep running.
questions.correct_explanation: A parallel test brings systems up at the recovery site and runs real work there while production carries on, so it proves the site works without risking an outage. A full interruption test is the runner-up: it is the most realistic test, but shutting the main site is exactly what the goal rules out, and it needs senior management approval because it can cause the outage it plans for.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because tabletops find gaps cheaply. But talking through steps cannot prove the system actually runs at the recovery site.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because checklists confirm the plan is complete. But reviewing documents proves nothing about whether the recovery site can run the system.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: it proves recovery most realistically. But it stops the main site, which the goal rules out, and risks a real outage.

tips: Eliminate: A and B are paper or discussion tests, which check the plan but cannot show the recovery site really runs the system.
Final two: D beats C because a parallel test proves the site while production keeps running; a full interruption stops production.
Exam cue: a parallel test adds the recovery site beside live production; a full interruption switches production off. If production must keep running, stop at parallel.

questions.question: A grocery chain's AI demand forecast drops to 79% accuracy, and its runbook, approved by the model owner, has the on-call technician switch stores to manual ordering below 85%. What should the technician do FIRST?

options.A: Ask the model owner to approve manual ordering, then wait
options.B: Switch stores to manual ordering, then tell the model owner
options.C: Retrain the current model on this month's data, then redeploy it
options.D: Restart the forecasting servers, then check whether accuracy recovers

questions.key_concept: When a model drifts past a set threshold, an approved runbook can give the switch to a fallback process to the practitioner on duty.
questions.pre_read: Check what the runbook says happens below the threshold, and who it names.
questions.correct_explanation: The runbook, approved by the model owner, gives the switch to manual ordering to the on-call technician once accuracy falls below 85%, and 79% is below it. So the technician acts in role: moves stores to the manual process, then tells the owner. Asking the owner to approve the switch is the runner-up: the owner does decide on retraining, but they already approved what happens below the threshold, and waiting leaves bad forecasts running.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the owner should hear about it. But they already approved manual ordering below 85% in the runbook; asking again and waiting keeps poor forecasts in use.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because retraining could fix drift. But retraining is the model owner's decision and takes time; the runbook calls for manual ordering now.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because restarts fix many faults. But drift means the model is losing accuracy on changed data; healthy servers still serve wrong forecasts.

tips: Eliminate: C takes over the owner's retraining decision, and D treats drift as a server fault, when the model itself is giving worse answers.
Final two: B beats A because the owner's approved runbook already gives the switch below 85% to the technician; asking again only delays it, and the owner is still told.
Exam cue: a drifting model is a continuity problem. When an approved runbook names the fallback and gives it to you, use it, then report.

questions.question: A newspaper's AI threat-monitoring tool keeps its tuned detection rules, settings and logs only on the servers it watches. What should the security analyst propose to BEST restore detection early in a ransomware recovery?

options.A: Add a second server with the same rules on the same network
options.B: Pause monitoring during recovery so restores finish sooner
options.C: Copy the tool's rules and settings to separate offline storage
options.D: Retrain the tool on fresh traffic once the servers are restored

questions.key_concept: Detection tools need their rules, settings and logs backed up away from the systems they watch, so monitoring survives the event.
questions.pre_read: Notice where the tool's knowledge lives and what ransomware would reach.
questions.correct_explanation: Ransomware that encrypts the watched servers would take the tool's tuned rules, settings and logs with them, leaving recovery unwatched. Copies kept away from those servers can be restored early, so detection works while systems come back. A second server on the same network is the runner-up: it helps if one machine fails, but the same attack can reach both.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a second server adds redundancy. But on the same network it can be encrypted in the same attack.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because recovery is busy. But attackers exploit the confusion, and restored systems need watching; monitoring belongs early in recovery.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the tool can learn again. But retraining takes time and loses months of tuning, leaving recovery poorly watched.

tips: Eliminate: B drops monitoring just when attackers exploit the confusion, and D loses months of tuning and leaves a blind period while the tool relearns.
Final two: C beats A because copies away from the watched servers survive the attack; a second server on the same network can be encrypted at the same time.
Exam cue: detection must survive the outage it warns about. Keep its rules, settings and logs apart from the systems it watches.

questions.question: A game studio employee reports a lost work phone two days late, saying they did not know who to tell or whether it counted. Which change should the security manager propose to BEST improve reporting?

options.A: Publish one simple reporting route with examples of what to report
options.B: Formally warn the employee for reporting the loss two days late
options.C: Add a module on looking after devices to every employee's yearly course
options.D: Turn on remote wipe for every work phone the studio issues

questions.key_concept: Reporting must be easy: one clear route and plain examples of what counts get incidents reported fast.
questions.pre_read: Notice why the report came late and what the manager wants to improve.
questions.correct_explanation: The delay came from not knowing where or what to report, and every hour a lost device goes unreported is time to misuse it. One simple route, with examples such as lost devices, wrong sends and odd messages, removes that doubt for everyone. A device-care module is the runner-up: it may cut losses, but the question asks about reporting, and care training does not tell staff where to report.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the delay did add risk. But punishing a reporter teaches everyone to hide mistakes, making future reports slower, or absent.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: it targets the loss itself. But the delay came from not knowing the route, not from careless handling.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because remote wipe limits harm from a lost phone. But it works only once someone reports the loss, and does nothing about why the report came late.

tips: Eliminate: B punishes the reporting the studio needs more of, and D adds a technical control that still waits on a report.
Final two: A beats C because the delay came from not knowing where to report; device training targets the loss, not the reporting.
Exam cue: fix the cause the stem names. If people report late because the route is unclear, make reporting simple and give examples.

questions.question: A city transit agency's awareness lead learns that a fake parcel-delivery text is targeting staff phones this week; the yearly course runs in six months. Which step is BEST for reaching all staff?

options.A: Rerun the full yearly security course for all staff this month
options.B: Send all staff a short alert now picturing the fake text
options.C: Give the help desk team role-based training on the parcel scam
options.D: Ask staff to forward the fake text to coworkers as a warning

questions.key_concept: Awareness reaches everyone with short, timely messages about current threats; training builds job skills for particular roles.
questions.pre_read: Notice who is targeted and how soon they need to know.
questions.correct_explanation: Awareness activities run all year and respond to current threats with short, timely messages for everyone. A brief alert now, showing what the text looks like and how to report it, reaches all staff while the scam is live. Rerunning the full course is the runner-up: it reaches everyone too, but it is slow and heavy for one new scam, and training time is better aimed at specific roles.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: it does reach every employee. But a full course is slow to organize and heavy for one live scam; a short alert does the job this week.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because role-based training builds skills. But this text targets every employee's phone, so training one team leaves everyone else unwarned.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it spreads the warning. But forwarding passes on the live lure and its link; warnings should come from the awareness lead.

tips: Eliminate: C trains one team for a scam aimed at everyone, and D spreads the live lure instead of a safe warning.
Final two: B beats A because awareness is short and timely for everyone; a full course is too slow and heavy for one live scam.
Exam cue: awareness is short, frequent and for everyone; training builds skills for particular roles. A new threat hitting everyone now calls for awareness.

questions.question: A mining company's security analyst sees that its chief financial officer received an email built from details of their conference talk, asking for a rushed payment. Which term names this attack MOST precisely?

options.A: A smishing attack
options.B: A vishing attack
options.C: A spear phishing attack
options.D: A whaling attack

questions.key_concept: Whaling is spear phishing aimed at senior executives, often seeking payments or sensitive data and built from public details about them.
questions.pre_read: Notice the channel used and who was targeted.
questions.correct_explanation: Whaling is spear phishing aimed at a senior executive, the 'big fish', often asking for payments or sensitive data and built from public details about the target. A chief financial officer targeted with details from their own talk fits exactly. Spear phishing is the runner-up: it is also tailored to one person, but whaling is the more precise name when the target is a top executive.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because smishing is a phishing variant. But smishing arrives by text message, and this lure came by email.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because vishing also targets individuals. But vishing uses voice calls, and this attack was an email.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the email is tailored to one person. But when that person is a senior executive, whaling is the more precise term.

tips: Eliminate: A and B name the wrong channel, text message and voice call, for a lure that came by email.
Final two: D beats C because whaling is spear phishing aimed at a senior executive, so it names this attack more precisely.
Exam cue: name the channel first (email, text, voice, QR code), then the target: one researched person is spear phishing; a top executive is whaling.

questions.question: A furniture maker's IT lead is preparing a monthly security report for managers. Which item is MOST accurately a metric rather than a raw measure?

options.A: 1,850 of 2,000 staff accounts have multifactor sign-in turned on
options.B: 340 suspicious emails were reported by staff this month
options.C: Staff accounts with multifactor sign-in: 92.5%, against a 98% target
options.D: Share of staff accounts with multifactor sign-in this month: 92.5%

questions.key_concept: A measure is a raw, quantified value; a metric compares measures with a set target to track progress and support decisions.
questions.pre_read: Think about what each item would let managers decide.
questions.correct_explanation: A measure is a raw, quantified value, such as a count or a share of accounts using multifactor sign-in. A metric uses measures to track progress against a set target, so the sign-in rate shown against its 98% goal tells managers how far they are from where they need to be. The bare percentage is the runner-up: it looks calculated, but without a target it cannot say whether 92.5% is good enough.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it is precise. But it is a single raw count; with no target, nobody can tell whether 1,850 is good or bad.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because reports show staff are alert. But it is a single raw count with no target, so managers cannot tell whether 340 is good or bad.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: a percentage looks like a finished metric. But 92.5% restates 1,850 of 2,000; with no target beside it, it shows where things stand, not progress toward a goal.

tips: Eliminate: A and B are single raw counts, of accounts and of reported emails, with no goal to judge either against.
Final two: C beats D because it sets 92.5% against the 98% target; tracking progress toward a set target is what defines a metric.
Exam cue: a measure is a raw number; a metric sets it against a target so it can drive a decision. Look for the target.

questions.question: A concert promoter's security manager must show the board what ransomware outages mean for the business. Which measure BEST fits this audience?

options.A: Revenue lost for each hour that ticket sales are offline
options.B: Average hours taken to restore the ticketing system
options.C: Share of servers with endpoint protection installed
options.D: Number of malware alerts the tools raised this quarter

questions.key_concept: Impact measures express security results in business terms, such as lost revenue, and suit boards and executives.
questions.pre_read: Notice who the audience is and what they decide.
questions.correct_explanation: Boards decide on money, mission and risk, so they need impact measures that turn security results into business terms. Revenue lost per hour of ticket-sales outage tells them directly what ransomware costs. Average restore time is the runner-up: it is a useful efficiency measure, but the board would still have to translate hours into business harm themselves.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: restore time matters and links to impact. But it is an efficiency measure for operators; the board needs the business cost those hours create.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because coverage shows a control exists. But it is an implementation measure and says nothing about what outages cost the business.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it shows activity. But an alert count reflects tool volume, not business effect, and means little to a board.

tips: Eliminate: C shows only that a control is installed, and D counts tool activity; neither says what outages cost.
Final two: A beats B because the board needs the business effect; restore time is an efficiency measure that still needs translating.
Exam cue: match the measure to the audience. Boards and executives want impact in business terms; operators want implementation and efficiency measures.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 3.3 (Types of Measures: implementation, effectiveness, efficiency and impact)

questions.question: A wind farm operator's draft quarterly report, owned by the security manager, shows 86% of servers patched, but the dashboard shows 91% for the same month. What should the reviewing analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Change the report to 91%, then tell the security manager
options.B: Release the report, since dashboards and reports often differ
options.C: Drop the patching figure from this quarter's report
options.D: Flag both figures and their data sources to the security manager

questions.key_concept: The same metric must show the same value in every view; a mismatch goes to the report's owner before release.
questions.pre_read: Notice who owns the report and what is still unknown about the two figures.
questions.correct_explanation: The same metric must show the same value in every view, so a gap between report and dashboard means a definition, query or cutoff differs. The analyst flags both figures and their sources to the security manager, who owns the report, before it goes out. Changing the report to 91% is the runner-up: it makes the views agree, but the dashboard might be the wrong one, and the report is not the analyst's to change.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the views must match. But nobody yet knows which figure is right, and the report belongs to the security manager, so the analyst flags it first.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because small differences seem normal. But leaders compare views, and an unexplained gap erodes trust in every number reported.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it avoids publishing a number that may be wrong. But it keeps the gap from leaders; the owner must learn the views disagree so the cause gets fixed.

tips: Eliminate: B releases numbers that disagree, and C drops a figure leaders rely on instead of tracing why the views differ.
Final two: D beats A because the cause is unknown and the report is the security manager's; flag both sources rather than picking one.
Exam cue: one metric, one value in every view. When views disagree, trace the sources and tell the owner before release.

questions.subtopic: 2.4 Measuring effectiveness. Using measurement to improve
questions.question: A sports stadium operator's monthly security report has grown to 45 metrics, and a review shows leaders used only 8 for any decision last year. What should the metrics analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Keep the full set of metrics so the report's history stays complete
options.B: Retire the 37 unused metrics and archive their past data
options.C: Add a one-page summary above the existing 45 metrics
options.D: Replace the current set with five new metrics chosen from scratch

questions.key_concept: Metrics that drive no decision should be retired deliberately, keeping their history, so effort goes to the ones that matter.
questions.pre_read: Notice how many metrics leaders actually use.
questions.correct_explanation: Metrics exist to drive decisions; ones nobody uses cost effort to collect and bury the eight that matter. Retiring them deliberately, with leaders' agreement and their history kept, makes the report sharper and frees effort for new risks. A summary page on top is the runner-up: it helps readers, but all 45 still have to be collected, checked and explained every month.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because history matters. But history can be kept while collection stops; keeping unused metrics live wastes effort and hides what matters.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: a summary does help leaders. But all 45 metrics still have to be gathered and checked each month, and the clutter remains.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it starts fresh. But it drops the eight metrics leaders actually use and breaks every trend they rely on.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps unused metrics running for completeness, and D throws out the eight metrics leaders actually use.
Final two: B beats C because retiring unused metrics removes the work and the clutter; a summary page only hides it.
Exam cue: a metric that drives no decision is a candidate to retire. Retire on purpose and keep the history; never keep or delete metrics by habit.
